name: Vandyke Red
lede: Vandyke Red is a dark brownish red; as a pigment name it is an old synonym for copper ferrocyanide, a chemical cousin of Prussian blue, and as a swatch it comes from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas.

sections.title: The pigment behind the name
sections.body:
The *Pigment Compendium* lists Vandyke red as a common name for copper ferrocyanide, also written copper hexacyanoferrate(II), and classes it as a red-brown [1][2]. The same compound travelled under many names: Hatchett's brown, Florence brown, prussiate of copper and Prussian brown [3][4][5]. Doerner (1935) treats Roman brown as another name for Florence brown [3].

Books and sources disagree on the exact formula. The compendium gives both Cu2Fe(CN)6 and CuK2Fe(CN)6, and adds that such hexacyanoferrates form a loose family in which other metals can substitute for the iron or copper [2][5]. Bersch (1901) gave a recipe for Hatchett's brown, the same material [4].

sections.title: Cousin of Prussian blue
sections.body: The compendium files copper hexacyanoferrate under the same hexacyanoferrate group as [[prussian-blue]], with a cross-reference between them [2][5]. The name is not the same as Vandyke brown, a separate [[brown]] pigment with its own entry, including a calcined form [6]. Who the Vandyke was and why the name was chosen is undocumented in the books we hold [6].

sections.title: The swatch is an atlas color
sections.body: The swatch comes from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, plate XIII, hue 1', tone k; ISCC-NBS block 19 and Maerz and Paul plate 6 K 4 (first recorded 1912) agree on the name [7]. Ridgway's plates are scans of aged paper, so the color is approximate, and no book links the swatch to the pigment's actual look [7]. The nearest names are [[tuscan-red]] and, in plain words, [[mahogany]], at 9.9 units [7]. The library also pairs it with the Japanese *kokiake*, a deep scarlet [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The hue is present in 207 of 23,781 paintings (0.87 per cent), more than 61 per cent of the named colors [8]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 14 of 945 paintings, 2.5 times the museums' baseline, and in a painting it is most often an accent (66 of 117) [8].

The earliest match dates to 1301, 611 years before the name's first record (Ridgway, 1912) [7][8]. That is a look-alike hue in an aged, varnished photograph, not proof that copper ferrocyanide was in use [8].

openers: Vandyke red is a copper cousin of Prussian blue: the same cyanide-iron chemistry, a brown-red result.
The earliest archive match (1301) predates the name by 611 years, a look-alike, not a pigment.
